# 134 · A window counter that advances by one window leaves its start behind a quiet client

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | medium | feature, behaviour change intended | [`Window#counted`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> Crosscut's `Window` record, the fixed-window request counter a rate-limiting filter keeps per client, gains a `previousCount` component for the sliding-window estimate (Cloudflare's approximation: the previous window's count weighted by how much of it the sliding window still covers). The counting method is rewritten with it: a request in the same window adds one, and a request after it opens the next window, carrying this window's count. The tests pass, polling one window after another. But a client quiet for two or more windows gets a window starting one window after its old one, behind the clock, with the count of a window long gone carried into the estimate: its next request opens yet another window, so the count never passes one and the limit never applies to it. The regression proof relates the new record result to the old one on the components they share, `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`, with the old counter built from the new components, and finds a request two windows ahead.

Tags: [resilience](../README.md#tag-resilience), [clocks-and-time](../README.md#tag-clocks-and-time), [dropped-case](../README.md#tag-dropped-case), [record-components](../README.md#tag-record-components), [signature-change](../README.md#tag-signature-change)

## The change

Add a `previousCount` component to the record and an `estimated(nowNanos, windowNanos)` method that weights it by how much of the previous window the sliding window still covers. `counted` is rewritten: `nowNanos - startNanos < windowNanos` keeps the window and adds one; otherwise the result is `new Window(startNanos + windowNanos, 1, count)`, the next window with this one's count as the previous count. The tests take the third component, and one is added for the estimate.

The developer declares which inputs the change is meant to affect: `windowNanos > 0 && this.startNanos % windowNanos != 0`. The verifier proves that every other input behaves as before, or shows one that does not.

The record the method belongs to changed, so the developer states how the previous version's receiver is built from the new parameters, and how it is called: `Window#counted(nowNanos, windowNanos)` on `new Window(this.startNanos, this.count)`. The verifier proves that on every input, the new method agrees with the previous one called that way, or shows one on which it does not.

The result changed its type or its meaning, so the developer states how the two results are related, `previous` being the result of `Window#counted` and `result` the new method's: `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`. The verifier proves that the relation holds on every input where both versions return, and that they throw alike where they throw, or shows an input on which they do not.

**Before** ([`Window.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit;

/**
 * A fixed-window request counter, the simplest rate limit: how many requests a client has made in the window its
 * last request fell in, with windows of one length aligned to the epoch (Spring Cloud Gateway's rate limiter keeps
 * such a count per key and window; Resilience4j's {@code RateLimiter} calls the window a cycle). The counter is a
 * value: the filter keeps one per client, replaces it on each request with what {@link #counted} returns, and
 * refuses the request when the count passes the limit. The clock reading and the window length are arguments, so
 * that the counter is a pure function.
 *
 * <p>A counter starts as {@code new Window(0, 0)}: no request yet, in the window at the epoch.
 */
public record Window(long startNanos, long count) {

    public Window {
        if (startNanos < 0 || count < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the start and the count must not be negative");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The counter after a request at {@code nowNanos}, with windows of {@code windowNanos}: one more in the same
     * window, or the first request of the window the reading falls in.
     */
    public Window counted(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long start = nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos;
        return start == startNanos ? new Window(startNanos, count + 1) : new Window(start, 1);
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit;

/**
 * A sliding-window request counter, the rate limit that does not let a client spend two limits at a window
 * boundary: how many requests a client has made in the window its last request fell in, and how many in the window
 * before it, with windows of one length aligned to the epoch (Spring Cloud Gateway's rate limiter keeps such a
 * count per key and window; Resilience4j's {@code RateLimiter} calls the window a cycle). The counter is a value:
 * the filter keeps one per client, replaces it on each request with what {@link #counted} returns, and refuses the
 * request when {@link #estimated} passes the limit. The clock reading and the window length are arguments, so that
 * the counter is a pure function.
 *
 * <p>A counter starts as {@code new Window(0, 0, 0)}: no request yet, in the window at the epoch.
 */
public record Window(long startNanos, long count, long previousCount) {

    public Window {
        if (startNanos < 0 || count < 0 || previousCount < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the start and the counts must not be negative");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The counter after a request at {@code nowNanos}, with windows of {@code windowNanos}: one more in the same
     * window, or the first request of the next window, with this window's count as the previous count.
     */
    public Window counted(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        if (nowNanos - startNanos < windowNanos) {
            return new Window(startNanos, count + 1, previousCount);
        }
        return new Window(startNanos + windowNanos, 1, count);
    }

    /**
     * The requests in the window of {@code windowNanos} ending at {@code nowNanos}, estimated as the current
     * window's count plus the previous window's count weighted by how much of that sliding window it covers
     * (the approximation Cloudflare's rate limiter uses).
     */
    public long estimated(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long elapsed = Math.min(windowNanos, nowNanos - startNanos);
        return count + previousCount * (windowNanos - elapsed) / windowNanos;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The two versions disagree. The prover found this input outside the declared change, and the generator replayed it on the JVM against both versions:

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0, previousCount=0], nowNanos=2, windowNanos=1), previously counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0], nowNanos=2, windowNanos=1)` | `Window[startNanos=2, count=1]` | `Window[startNanos=1, count=1, previousCount=0]` |

One disagreeing input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `this: Window(startNanos: long, count: long, previousCount: long) × nowNanos: long × windowNanos: long`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A client that pauses for two windows or more is never rate-limited again until it sends two requests within one window of its own stale start, and its sliding-window estimate carries the count of a window long gone: the limit is both too loose for a bursty client that paused and too tight right after the pause. The filter's job is the limit, and the counter is where it lives.

## Why the verdict is right

The old method aligns the window's start to the clock, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`, so a request after any gap lands in the window it falls in. The new one keeps the window while `nowNanos - startNanos < windowNanos` and otherwise moves the start by exactly one window, `startNanos + windowNanos`, which is the window the request falls in only when the gap is shorter than two windows. The proof's witness, within the aligned starts, is a request two windows ahead of an empty counter, `counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0, previousCount=0], nowNanos=2, windowNanos=1)`: the old counter is `Window[startNanos=2, count=1]`, the new one `Window[startNanos=1, count=1, previousCount=0]`, a window behind. The harness builds the old record from the new components, calls both versions, and reads the two results' components into the relation `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`, which fails on the start. JBMC finds it in a fraction of a second searching inputs in [0:20], as `nowNanos=19, windowNanos=2`, shrunk in 24 interpreter runs.

## What to do

Keep the start aligned to the clock, and carry the count only into the window right after the one the counter was in, as example 135 does: `start - startNanos == windowNanos ? count : 0`.

## Notes

- The counter's start is aligned to the window: a counter begins as `Window(0, 0)` and every start the old method produces is `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. A start that is not aligned is no state the filter can hold, so the scope leaves those inputs out (`windowNanos > 0 && this.startNanos % windowNanos != 0` is the intended-change expression, used as the module's precondition is in 125, 132 and 133). Without the scope the first witness is an unaligned start, `counted(this=Window[startNanos=1, count=0, previousCount=0], nowNanos=1, windowNanos=2)`, which the old method realigns to zero and the new one keeps.
- The relation is over the components both records have. A record result of other components has no previous result to compare to: `resultsAgreeWhen` names each record's components as `previous.c` and `result.c`, read from the two records into the relation's locals, and the harness treats two null records as agreeing and one null alone as not. The old counter is built from the new components as in 130 and 131, `new Window(this.startNanos, this.count), nowNanos, windowNanos`.
- The new component is outside the relation: whether `previousCount` is right is not what this proof is about, only that the start and the count are what they were. A relation over `result.previousCount` alone would have to say what the old method, which had no such count, implies for it, and it implies nothing.
- The tests poll consecutive windows, where advancing by one window and realigning to the clock agree; the defect needs a gap of two windows or more, or a window length that does not divide the clock reading the counter started at.
- A counter left behind the clock is not only a wrong estimate: each later request finds `nowNanos - startNanos >= windowNanos` again and opens another window at one, so the client is never refused, and the carried count is the one from before its silence.
- The scope's guard matters: `this.startNanos % windowNanos != 0` alone divides by zero where the window is zero, in the scope expression itself, before either version runs. JBMC then reports a counterexample with `windowNanos=0` that does not reproduce (both versions throw `IllegalArgumentException` there), and the tool's own checker refuses the harness as outside its fragment, an uncaught `ArithmeticException` leaving it. With `windowNanos > 0 &&` first, the remainder is only taken where it is defined.
- JBMC finds the witness in a fraction of a second. When this example was written the tool's own checker did not: without the scope it found the unaligned-start witness in about 13 s (5 paths, 13 solver calls, nearly all of it in the SAT solver on the two 64-bit remainders), and with the scope, whose `this.startNanos % windowNanos` is a third remainder over other operands, it did not finish within two minutes. The time went into one solver call: refuting the side of `start == startNanos` that the scope makes infeasible, which is proving that one value is not a multiple of another through two divider circuits, something JBMC's one formula never has to do. Since then the checker asks about a branch's other side only for as long as its calls so far took (at least a second) and leaves an undecided side for after the decided paths, and it leaves a division to the solver under cheap facts, building the circuit only where a model got it wrong: it finds this example's witness under the scope in 2.4 s (5 paths, 16 solver calls, both remainders built in full), `counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=16, previousCount=16], nowNanos=16, windowNanos=8)` shrunk to the one above. The example still names JBMC, which is faster here, where 135 names the checker.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.3 s searching inputs in [0:20] as counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0, previousCount=0], nowNanos=19, windowNanos=2), shrunk to the input above in 24 interpreter runs, replayed in the interpreter; domain this: Window(startNanos: long, count: long, previousCount: long) × nowNanos: long × windowNanos: long.

```java
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
```

**Provenance:** Constructed on a new kernel of Crosscut, the fixed-window request counter, to show a regression proof across a change of a record result's components finding a defect the tests miss.

- [Cloudflare: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (the sliding window approximation over two fixed windows)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

```bash
python3 examples/tools/build.py 134
```
